description: Solo builder from Muscat taking on Flame in Freefall. I am a Computer Science student who builds AI-powered web dashboards and data tools. My focus: turning NASA's combustion data into clear, trustworthy fire safety insights for future Moon and Mars crews. Working solo, not seeking members at the moment. Languages: Arabic and English.
summary: Understudy Earth answers one question: where and when on Earth can we rehearse for the Moon and Mars? You pick a Moon or Mars place (for example Jezero crater or Shackleton rim) and a test (rover drive, instrument test, walking test, cold test, or a typed sentence). The app shows WHERE: 10 km Earth squares whose terrain shape (slope, roughness, relief) matches that place, using NASA LOLA and MOLA with ESA Copernicus DEM. It shows WHEN: the months whose temperature, wind, dryness and sunlight suit the test, from NASA POWER. It is honest: when nothing we searched is close enough, the map turns grey and says "no qualifying candidate". Results open as a card with a 12-month strip, a 3D view and a printable one-page Test Site Brief. You can also click or type any spot on Mars or the lunar poles to see where it fits on Earth. We checked it against random squares and known sites such as AMADEE-18 in Dhofar, Oman. It is a static web app with no login and no server, and it works on a phone. It is a screening aid, not a validated site selector.
details:
What it does. Understudy Earth helps planners choose where and when to rehearse a Moon or Mars job on Earth. The user picks a Moon or Mars target and describes the test. The app ranks Earth squares by terrain match and shows the best months for that test.

How it works. Moon, Mars and Earth elevation are averaged to 500 m cells and cut into 10 km squares. Each square gets slope, roughness and relief numbers. A six-term terrain distance, scaled by the spread across all Earth squares, ranks squares for the chosen target. A gap test compares the best distance with distances between random Earth pairs, so a top rank is never called a twin: if nothing is close enough, the app says "no qualifying candidate in the searched area". Months come from NASA POWER climatology (temperature, wind, humidity, sunlight) against the test's needs. Where and when colour is the worse of the terrain tier and the best-month tier.

Benefits and impact. Mission planners, analog programs and students can screen sites with numbers, see the best time of year, and print a one-page brief. Oman is the local story: Dhofar hosted the AMADEE-18 Mars simulation in February 2018.

Checks. A baseline against random squares (AMADEE-18 area median rank 21% and Meteor Crater 18% for Mars, random about 50%), a name-free check, a stability check across 8 settings (only 4 of 17 targets keep the same tier, so each result is marked robust or threshold-sensitive), a land-cover mask and a second slope method. These are retrospective sanity checks, not independent validation.

Also built. Click or type any spot on Mars (87 S to 87 N) or the lunar poles; a world view of 45 places; fine-scale Jezero and Gale checks; a rough-proxy surface material panel (THEMIS thermal inertia, GLiM rock type, temperature swing), context only and not scored; a calendar and two-site plan; a share link.

Limits. Terrain shape only: no geology, gravity, air or radiation match. 500 m cells hide rocks and steps. Climate is a typical-year average on coarse cells. Ready-made test needs are our assumptions.

Tools. Python (numpy, scipy, rasterio, pyproj) precomputes the data. The app is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet, hosted on GitHub Pages. There is no AI at runtime.

LIVE WEBSITE LINK : https://samaralhadhrami.github.io/understudy-earth/
